lessons.title: Clothes and colours: what are you wearing?
lessons.goal: Name clothes with der, die or das and the plural, say what you wear with tragen and what you need with brauchen, and name colours after sein.

grammar.point: tragen (to wear) changes a to ä for du and er/sie. The clothes are the accusative object: only der-words change (einen Mantel). We use die Jeans as a plural: Die Jeans sind blau.
grammar.oneLine: Ich trage einen Mantel. Du trägst eine Jacke. Die Jeans sind blau.

mistake.why: The a changes to ä for du and er/sie, like fahren: du fährst, er fährt.

terms.meaning: to wear (with clothes) or to carry
the vowel changes in the du and er/sie forms: a becomes ä
a word we use as a plural, like die Jeans (you also hear eine Jeans)
a pair: ein Paar Schuhe

cards.title: Before we start: what are you wearing today?
cards.body: Chapter 11 is about clothes and shopping: on a trip to Berlin, Mira and Ben look for something to wear to Anna's party. Today you say what you wear and what you need. You know Ich esse einen Apfel: only der-words change. Clothes work the same way.

examples.why: You know this already.
New today: tragen + a clothes word.

steps: You already know: der, die, das and einen Apfel, eine Banane, ein Ei (chapters 2 and 4)
New today: clothes words with their article, and the verb tragen (to wear)
By the end you can: say what you wear and what you need, in winter and in summer
cards.more: Think of a wardrobe with labels. Each piece of clothing has a label: der, die or das. You already know how to read these labels from chapter 2, and you know that after a verb like essen only the der-words change: einen Apfel. Today you fill a wardrobe with nine pieces and learn one new verb, tragen, which means to wear. The sentence is built exactly like Ich esse einen Apfel. You will learn it step by step in the next cards, one small piece at a time.

cards.title: Clothes: learn der, die or das
cards.body: Every piece of clothing has a gender. Learn the article together with the word: der Pullover, die Jacke, das Hemd. Jeans is special: we use it as a plural, die Jeans sind … (you will also hear eine Jeans).
cards.more: Imagine three coat hooks: a blue one for der, a pink one for die and a green one for das. Every piece of clothing hangs on one hook. Nobody can tell you which hook just by looking at the coat, so you learn the hook together with the word. That is why we always write der Mantel, not just Mantel. Jeans is a trick word: it is like trousers in English, always more than one leg, so we use it as a plural: die Jeans sind blau.
cards.lead: In the last card you met the idea of clothes words. On this card: the nine words and their articles, so you can name what Mira, Ben and Leon wear.

deeper.text: Many words for clothes with a soft ending like -e are feminine: die Jacke, die Hose. But there are many exceptions, for example der Käse. So do not guess: say the article every time you learn a word, out loud, as one piece.

cards.title: More than one: plurals of clothes
cards.body: More than one piece of clothing: die + the plural form, and the verb is sind. Pullover stays the same. Jacke gets -n, Hemd gets -en, Kleid gets -er, Rock gets an umlaut and -e, Mantel only an umlaut. A pair of shoes is ein Paar Schuhe: learn it as one chunk.

examples.en: That is a pair of shoes.

cards.more: You know the plural from chapter 2: die plus a new ending, and sind instead of ist. Clothes follow the same five patterns. Some words just add something at the end, some change the vowel with two dots, and Pullover does nothing at all. Because there is no way to guess, you learn the plural together with the word, like a pair of socks you never separate. Jeans looks the same in the plural, so it needs no change. A Paar is like a pair of shoes in English: ein Paar Schuhe.
cards.lead: You can name the nine clothes words now. On this card: their plural forms, so you can talk about more than one jacket, one pair of shoes or all your jeans.

deeper.text: A plural word always takes die, whether the single word was der, die or das. Look at die Röcke and die Kleider: the article changed to die, the noun changed too. In a plural sentence the verb is sind, not ist. Say the plural out loud together with the word until it feels natural.

cards.title: tragen: a → ä
cards.body: tragen means to wear. It changes a to ä for du and er/sie, just like fahren in chapter 2: ich trage, du trägst, er trägt. The other forms keep the a. tragen also means to carry, as in Kisten tragen. With clothes it means to wear.
cards.more: A verb can have a little costume change. With tragen the costume change is two dots on the a: du trägst and er trägt wear the dots, but ich trage, wir tragen and sie tragen do not. You have seen exactly this with fahren: ich fahre, du fährst, er fährt. So you do not learn something brand new, you just say: tragen is a fahren-verb. And when you read tragen next to clothes, it means wear, not carry.
cards.lead: You know the clothes words. On this card: the new verb tragen with all six forms, so you can say what you, Mira or we wear.

deeper.text: Why only du and er/sie? In German, some very common verbs change their vowel in exactly those two forms, and you already know fahren, schlafen and essen. The umlaut in trägst and trägt is easy to hear. When you listen to a German speaker, an ä in a verb form after du or er tells you it may be one of these vowel-changing verbs: fährt, schläft, trägt. Use the sentence to know which verb it is.

cards.title: What do you wear? tragen + accusative
cards.body: The clothes are the object of tragen, so you use the accusative from chapter 4: only the der-words change. Ich trage einen Mantel. Die and das words stay: eine Jacke, ein Hemd. Jeans has no article. Ask: Was trägst du heute?
cards.more: Picture a little machine: you put in a clothes word, and a sentence comes out. If the word is a der-word, the machine says einen. If it is a die-word, it says eine. A das-word gets ein. A word like Jeans gets nothing, because it is plural and has no ein. That is exactly the machine from chapter 4 with food, only the food is now a coat. To ask, you say Was trägst du heute? and the answer starts with Ich trage.
cards.lead: You can make the forms of tragen now. On this card: tragen with a clothes word as the object, so you can say what you wear and ask a friend the same.

deeper.text: A question about the object uses the question word was in position 1 and the verb in part 2, like Was isst du? from chapter 4. The answer repeats the verb: Was trägst du? Ich trage einen Pullover. Notice that trägst changes to trage when you answer, because du becomes ich.

cards.title: Colours: it is blue, it is red
cards.body: Say the colour after sein, with no ending: Die Jacke ist grün. The shoes are plural: Die Schuhe sind schwarz. Do not put the colour before the noun yet. Use two short sentences instead: Ich trage ein Hemd. Es ist weiß.

examples.de: Ich trage ein Hemd. Es ist weiß.
examples.en: I wear a shirt. It is white.

cards.more: You already used colours in chapter 9, when you said Das Sofa ist grün. Clothes work the same way. Think of two small steps: first you say what you wear, then you say what colour it is, in a second short sentence. That way the colour word never has to change. After sein a colour stays exactly as it is in the list: rot, blau, grün, gelb, schwarz, weiß, braun, grau. In the plural you only change the verb, from ist to sind.
cards.lead: You can say what you wear. On this card: eight colours after sein, so you can tell what colour your jacket or shoes are.

deeper.text: Germans make shades of a colour with hell (light) and dunkel (dark): hellblau, dunkelblau, hellgrün. You glue the word to the front, and after sein it still takes no ending. Before a noun a colour does take an ending (eine rote Jacke), but that comes later. For now, keep the colour after sein.

cards.title: Winter and summer: time first
cards.body: Start with the time to say when: Im Winter, Im Sommer. The verb is still part 2, and the subject comes after it: Im Winter trage ich einen Mantel. For too cold or too warm, use zu: Die Jacke ist zu warm.

examples.de: Im Winter trage ich einen Mantel.
examples.en: In winter I wear a coat.

examples.de: Im Sommer trage ich ein Kleid.
examples.en: In summer I wear a dress.

examples.de: Im Sommer trägt Ben keine Jacke.
examples.en: In summer Ben does not wear a jacket.

examples.de: Im Sommer ist die Jacke zu warm.
examples.en: In summer the jacket is too warm.

steps: Start with the time: Im Winter
Put the verb in part 2: trage
Add the subject: ich
Add the clothes: einen Mantel. Im Winter trage ich einen Mantel.
cards.more: A German sentence is like a train with a fixed second carriage: the verb always sits there. You can put anything in the first carriage: ich, or a time like im Winter. If the time takes the first carriage, then ich has to move behind the verb: Im Winter trage ich. That is not a new rule, you know it from chapter 3 and chapter 4. The clothes only give you a lovely new thing to talk about: what you wear in which season.
cards.lead: Now you can say what you wear. On this card: starting with im Winter or im Sommer, so you can tell when you wear each piece of clothing.

deeper.text: Watch the difference between sehr and zu. Sehr warm only means very warm, and that can be good in winter. Zu warm means too warm: it is a problem, you do not want it. So a shop assistant hears zu and knows at once that something is wrong. Use zu for complaints and sehr for praise.

example.de: Der Mantel ist sehr warm, aber nicht zu warm.
example.en: The coat is very warm, but not too warm.

cards.title: I need ...: brauchen + accusative
cards.body: brauchen takes the accusative too: Ich brauche eine Hose. Brauchst du einen Pullover? A yes/no question starts with the verb. For nothing, use keine: Wir brauchen keine Schuhe. Pick der, die or das first, then einen, eine or ein.
cards.more: This last card is a mini-game with three steps. Step one: is the thing a der-word, a die-word or a das-word? Step two: because it is the object, turn der into einen, and keep eine and ein. Step three: put the verb in the right place. You know all three steps already, from chapter 3 and chapter 4. This card just brings the new clothes words and the verbs tragen and brauchen together, so you can say what you need for a party.
cards.lead: You have all the pieces now. On this last card: brauchen with the same accusative rule, so you can say what you need and ask a friend what they need.

deeper.text: When you do not need something, kein is a better answer than nicht. Kein works like ein: keinen for a der-word, keine for a die-word and a plural, kein for a das-word. Wir brauchen keine Schuhe says you do not need any shoes. You know kein from chapter 3 and keinen from chapter 4.

lessons.title: Welcher Pullover? Which one?
lessons.goal: Ask which thing with welcher, welche, welches and welchen, ask for size and colour, and answer with Den hier or Die da.

grammar.point: welch- (which?) works like der, die, das: welcher (m), welche (f), welches (n), welche (plural). For an object only the masculine changes: welchen.
grammar.oneLine: Welcher Pullover ist grün? Welchen Mantel nimmst du? Den hier.

mistake.why: Mantel is masculine and the object of the verb, so welch- gets -en: welchen.

terms.meaning: the question word for which: welcher, welche, welches
der, die or das with hier, da or dort, for example Den hier.
size (of clothes) or height

cards.title: Before we start: which one do you mean?
cards.body: In a shop you do not only say what you need, you also ask which one: Welche Jacke? Welchen Mantel? Today you learn welch-, a question word that works like der, die, das. You know that der becomes den for an object. Welch- does the same.

examples.why: You know this already: der becomes den.
New today: welchen asks which.

steps: You already know: der, die, das, and der becomes den for an object (chapters 2 and 4)
New today: welcher, welche, welches (which?) and welchen for an object
By the end you can: ask Welche Jacke? and Welchen Mantel? and answer Den hier.
cards.more: Think of a shop with many coats on a rail. A friend points at the rail, and you want to know which coat they mean. In English you say which coat. In German you say welcher, welche or welches, depending on the gender, just like der, die and das. You already know that for an object only the der-word changes: der becomes den. Welcher becomes welchen in the same way. You will learn it step by step in the next cards.

cards.title: Which? A question word for things
cards.body: welch- means which. It stands in position 1 together with its noun, and the verb is part 2, as in every W-question from chapter 1. Welche Jacke ist das? Welcher Pullover ist grün? The word welch- needs an ending, and you learn the endings on the next card.
steps: Start with welch- and the noun: Welche Jacke
Put the verb in part 2: ist
Add the rest: das? Welche Jacke ist das?
cards.more: A question word is like a flashlight: it points at the missing piece of information. Wie points at how, wo points at where, and welch- points at which one out of several things. With welch- you always say the noun right behind it, so the flashlight lights up the right coat: welche Jacke, welcher Pullover. Everything else is the same as in chapter 1: the question word group comes first, and the verb sits in the second place.
cards.lead: In the introduction you saw welchen in a question. On this card: welch- + noun as the first part of a question, so you can ask which piece of clothing someone means.

deeper.text: In English, which usually stands alone or before the noun, too: which coat? In German, welch- also stays right before the noun, and the pair forms position 1. So the verb never comes between them. You say Welche Jacke ist teuer? and never Welche ist Jacke teuer.

cards.title: welch- ends like der, die, das
cards.body: welch- takes an ending that matches the gender of the noun: der Pullover gives welcher, die Jacke gives welche, das Hemd gives welches. For more than one, you use welche. So the ending copies the end of der, die, das.
cards.more: Look at the end of der, die, das: the letters are -er, -ie and -as. Welcher, welche and welches copy these endings: -er, -e, -es. It is like a secret code: the article tells you the gender, and welch- borrows the sound. For a der-word you hear -er, for a das-word you hear -es, and for a die-word or a plural you hear -e. Learn it as a little song: welcher, welche, welches, welche.
cards.lead: You know the idea of welch-. On this card: its four forms, one for each gender and one for the plural, so you can ask about any piece of clothing.

deeper.text: Notice what stays the same: the root welch-. Only the end changes, and it follows the gender of the noun. Das Kleid is a das-word, so you say welches Kleid. If you are not sure about the ending, first say the noun with der, die or das, and then borrow its sound.

cards.title: welchen: the masculine object
cards.body: When the thing is the object, only the masculine form changes: welcher becomes welchen, like der becomes den. Welchen Mantel nimmst du? The others stay: Welche Hose brauchst du? Welches Hemd trägst du? Welche Schuhe trägst du?

examples.en: Which sweater are you wearing today?

cards.more: You learned the accusative rule in chapter 4: only the masculine changes. Welch- follows this rule exactly. If the clothes word is a der-word and the object of the verb, you add -en: welchen Mantel. That is why a question like Welchen Mantel nimmst du? starts with welchen. For die-words, das-words and the plural, welch- looks the same as before. One small change for one gender, that is all.
cards.lead: You know welcher, welche and welches. On this card: welchen, the form for a masculine object, so you can ask which coat or which sweater someone takes.

deeper.text: The question starts with the object, so the verb is part 2, and the subject du comes right after it. Welchen Mantel nimmst du? In a plain statement you would say Du nimmst den Mantel. Same words, other order. Both sentences use the accusative: the coat is the object.

cards.title: Answer: der hier, den da
cards.body: A short answer uses der, die or das, with hier, da or dort to point: Welche Hose ist teuer? Die da. For the masculine object use den: Welchen Pullover nimmst du? Den hier. You do not repeat the noun.

examples.de: Welche Hose ist teuer? Die da.
examples.en: Which trousers are expensive? Those there.

examples.de: Welchen Pullover nimmst du? Den hier.
examples.en: Which sweater do you take? This one here.

examples.de: Welches Hemd ist neu? Das dort.
examples.en: Which shirt is new? That one over there.

cards.more: When you point at something in a shop, you do not repeat the whole noun, because you and the seller can both see it. You say der, die or das with a place word: hier for here, da for there, dort for over there. The article works like a pointing finger. Only for a masculine object, the finger says den: den hier. It is the same rule from chapter 4, only the words are shorter. You already know hier, da and dort from chapter 3.
cards.lead: You can ask with welch-. On this card: short answers like Den hier and Die da, so you can answer without repeating the noun, just like in a real shop.

deeper.text: In a short answer, der, die and das are not just the, they mean this one. You often say them a bit louder, as if you point a finger. Hier means near me, da and dort mean farther away. A native speaker can answer Welche Jacke? with just Die da, and everyone understands.

example.de: Welchen Mantel brauchst du? Den da.
example.en: Which coat do you need? That one there.

cards.title: Small clothes
cards.body: Here are ten more words for the shop. Learn each with its article and plural. Kleidung means clothes in general and has no plural. Paar means a pair. Ask about them with welch-: Welche Mütze brauchst du? Welchen Gürtel nimmst du?
cards.more: Your wardrobe is bigger than nine pieces. Here are ten small things you also meet in a shop: a T-shirt, a sock, a cap, a scarf, a blouse, a suit, a belt, a glove, a pair and clothes in general. Each word has its own hook: der, die or das. Look at the plural column too: Socke becomes Socken, Anzug gets an umlaut, and Gürtel does not change at all. Kleidung is special: it is like the word clothing in English, it has no plural.
cards.lead: You can ask which clothes someone means. On this card: ten smaller clothes words with their articles and plurals, so you can shop for socks, a scarf or a belt.

deeper.text: A Paar is two things that belong together: ein Paar Socken, ein Paar Handschuhe. After a Paar you do not use an article, you just say the plural noun. Kleidung is feminine and singular, so the verb is ist: Die Kleidung ist neu.

example.en: I need a pair of gloves.

cards.title: Welche Größe? Welche Farbe?
cards.body: In a shop you also ask about size and colour. Welche Größe haben Sie? Ich habe Größe 40. Welche Farbe hat die Jacke? Sie ist grün. Größe and Farbe are die-words, so you use welche. Farbe means colour. haben takes an object.

examples.en: Which colour does the jacket have?

cards.more: A seller wants to know two things: how big you are, and what colour you like. Both words are die-words, so the question starts with welche. Größe you know from chapter 8, where it meant how tall someone is. In a shop it also means the size of clothes, with a number: Größe 38, Größe 40, Größe 42. The question uses haben, and the answer repeats it: Ich habe Größe 40. For the colour you answer with sein: Sie ist grün.
cards.lead: You know the small clothes words. On this card: asking and saying size and colour, so you can talk to a seller in a clothes shop.

deeper.text: Sie with a capital S is the polite you, and its verb has the same form as wir and sie (they): haben, like heißen in Wie heißen Sie? from chapter 1. With a friend you say Welche Größe hast du? In the answer, size is just a number after Größe, no article. Sie ist grün answers about a die-word, so you use sie.

cards.title: Choose between two
cards.body: Offer two things with oder: Welchen Mantel nimmst du, den hier oder den da? Answer with nehmen and the short form: Ich nehme den hier. The masculine object is den again. For die, das and the plural: die, das, die.

examples.de: Welchen Mantel nimmst du, den hier oder den da?
examples.en: Which coat do you take, this one or that one?

examples.de: Welche Hose nimmst du, die hier oder die da?
examples.en: Which trousers do you take, these or those?

cards.more: This is what really happens in a shop: you hold two coats, one in each hand, and you cannot decide. The question has two halves, linked by oder. In the first half you ask welchen Mantel. In the second half you offer the choice with den hier and den da, like two pointing fingers. The answer is short: Ich nehme den hier. Only the masculine form changes to den, all other words stay as they are. This card puts together welch-, short answers and nehmen.
cards.lead: This is the last card of the lesson, and it brings everything together. You use welchen, a short answer with oder, and nehmen, so you can choose between two things in a shop.

deeper.text: The comma after du is normal in German: it separates the two parts of the question. After oder, the second part is short: den da. You do not need a verb there because it is clear from the first part. You know oder from chapter 7, and nehmen from chapter 4.

example.de: Welches Hemd nimmst du, das hier oder das da?
example.en: Which shirt do you take, this one or that one?

lessons.title: Dieser, diese, dieses: this one
lessons.goal: Point at clothes with dieser, diese, dieses and diesen, describe them with sein and an adjective, and say what you take with nehmen.

grammar.point: dies- (this, these) has the same endings as welch-: dieser (m), diese (f), dieses (n), diese (plural). For an object only the masculine changes: diesen. Unlike ein, dies- always has an ending.
grammar.oneLine: Dieser Pullover ist bequem. Ich nehme diesen Mantel.

mistake.why: Mantel is masculine and the object of the verb, so dies- gets -en: diesen.

terms.meaning: the pointing word for this or these: dieser, diese, dieses
a word with the endings of der, die, das, like welch- and dies-
to take; e becomes i for du and er/sie

cards.title: Before we start: this jacket, these shoes
cards.body: In a shop you point at things: this jacket, these shoes. In German the pointing word is dies-. You know welch- from lesson 2: welcher, welchen. Dies- has exactly the same endings. So one new word costs you almost nothing.

examples.why: You know this already.
New today: diesen points at it.

steps: You already know: welcher, welche, welches, welchen, and ein becomes einen (lesson 2 and chapter 4)
New today: dieser, diese, dieses (this, these) and diesen for a masculine object
By the end you can: point at clothes, describe them with sein and say Ich nehme diesen Mantel.
cards.more: Imagine you hold a coat and show it to a friend. Which coat? This coat! German uses a pointing word for this, dies-, and it wears exactly the same endings as welch-: dieser, diese, dieses, and diesen for a masculine object. If you can ask Welchen Mantel?, you can answer Diesen Mantel. So the question and the answer fit together like two puzzle pieces. You will learn the forms step by step in the next cards, and then you use them to describe and choose clothes.

cards.title: Point: dieser means this
cards.body: dies- means this, or these in the plural. It has four forms: dieser Pullover, diese Jacke, dieses Hemd, diese Schuhe. The ending matches the gender, as with welch-. Use it to point at a thing: Dieser Pullover ist schön.
cards.more: When you stand in a shop and point at a pullover, you say this pullover. In German this is dieser Pullover. The pointing word has to match the gender of the noun, so it changes: dieser for a der-word, diese for a die-word, dieses for a das-word and diese for the plural. The root is dies- and only the end changes. Say the four forms out loud together with a clothes word: dieser Pullover, diese Jacke, dieses Hemd, diese Schuhe.
cards.lead: In the introduction you saw diesen in one sentence. On this card: the four basic forms of dies-, so you can point at a coat, a jacket, a shirt or shoes.

deeper.text: Dies- is not the same as der, die, das. The plain article just says the, but dies- points at a thing, like a finger. In English you can also stress it: this one. When you say it in a shop, you often look at the thing and stress the word dieser or diese.

cards.title: dies- = welch-
cards.body: Dies- has exactly the same endings as welch-: -er, -e, -es, -e. So you can answer a welch- question with a dies- word: Welchen Mantel nimmst du? Diesen. The two words are partners: one asks which, the other points at this one.

examples.en: Which coat do you take? This one.
Which dress is new? This one.

examples.de: Welche Schuhe sind teuer? Diese hier.
examples.en: Which shoes are expensive? These here.

cards.more: Here is a nice trick. If you know welch-, you know dies-, because the endings are the same. Look at the table: welcher and dieser, welche and diese, welches and dieses. They are like twins who wear the same clothes at the end. When someone asks you Welches Kleid? you can use the ending of welches and say dieses. So you only have to learn one set of endings, and you use it for two words.
cards.lead: You know the four forms of dies-. On this card: how dies- and welch- share the same endings, so you can answer a which question with a this one.

deeper.text: The same endings also come from der, die, das. So three word families share one pattern: der, welcher, dieser. That is why Germans call these words der-words. You do not have to use that name, but it explains why the endings feel familiar.

example.de: Welcher Schal ist warm? Dieser hier.
example.en: Which scarf is warm? This one here.

cards.title: diesen: the masculine object
cards.body: For an object, only the masculine form changes: dieser becomes diesen, like der becomes den and welcher becomes welchen. Ich nehme diesen Mantel. Ich brauche diesen Gürtel. The others stay: diese Hose, dieses Hemd, diese Schuhe.
cards.more: You know the accusative rule from chapter 4, and from lesson 2: only the masculine changes. It happens again with dies-. If the thing is a der-word and the object, you add -en: diesen Mantel, diesen Gürtel, diesen Schal. For a die-word, a das-word and the plural, the form stays the same: diese Hose, dieses Hemd, diese Schuhe. So when you buy something, ask yourself: is it a der-word? Then say diesen. Otherwise you say the form you already know.
cards.lead: You can point with dies-. On this card: diesen, the form for a masculine object, so you can say which coat, belt or scarf you take or need.

deeper.text: A common mistake is to use the subject form for the object: Ich nehme dieser Mantel. To check, ask who does what. I take the coat, so I am the subject and the coat is the object. A der-word in the object place needs -en. The thing that gets taken, needed or worn is always the object.

cards.title: ein or dieser? Spot the difference
cards.body: Look at the nominative: ein Pullover has no ending, but dieser Pullover has -er. Ein Hemd has no ending, but dieses Hemd has -es. The rule: dies- always has an ending. Ein shows no ending for a der-word or a das-word. This is the big difference.
cards.more: Compare two little boxes. The box with ein is open at the end: ein Pullover, ein Hemd. Nothing is added. The box with dies- is always closed with a lid: dieser, dieses. The lid is the ending. For a die-word both boxes have a lid: eine Jacke, diese Jacke. So whenever you write dies-, add an ending. Whenever you write ein for a der-word or a das-word in the nominative, add nothing. Check the table and say each pair out loud.
cards.lead: You know ein and dies- now. On this card: the one big difference between them in the nominative, so you never forget the ending of dieser and dieses.

deeper.text: Why does ein have no ending for der-words and das-words? That is simply how ein works: ein Pullover, ein Hemd, kein Pullover, kein Hemd. You know this from chapter 3. Dies- always shows the gender clearly. The ending is its only job.

cards.title: Describe clothes: sein + adjective
cards.body: Say what clothes are like with sein and an adjective, with no ending: Dieser Pullover ist sehr bequem. Diese Hose ist zu eng. Dieses Hemd ist nicht teuer. Sehr means very, zu means too, nicht means not. They stand right before the adjective. Good quality is die Qualität.
cards.more: Now you can point at a thing and say what it is like. The recipe has three parts: the thing (dieser Pullover), the verb sein, and a describing word like bequem or eng. You learned this in chapter 3, when you described places: Der Hafen ist groß. Nothing is added to the adjective after sein. Words like sehr, zu and nicht go right before it, and they change the meaning: very comfortable, too tight, not expensive. Nine new adjectives are in the table.
cards.lead: You can point at clothes now. On this card: nine adjectives after sein, so you can say whether a jacket is comfortable, cheap or too tight.

deeper.text: Some adjectives are opposites: billig and teuer, eng and bequem, altmodisch and elegant. Learn them in pairs and they stick better. Günstig is a friendlier word than billig: it means good value, while billig can sound like cheap quality. In shops you often hear günstig.

cards.title: Say what you take: nehmen
cards.body: nehmen means to take. It changes e to i for du and er/sie, and the m doubles: ich nehme, du nimmst, er nimmt. Say what you take: Ich nehme diese Jacke. Nimmst du dieses Kleid? To say no, put nicht at the end: Ich nehme dieses Hemd nicht.

examples.en: I do not take this shirt.

cards.more: This is the step of shopping where you decide and say which one you take. The verb is nehmen, and you know it from chapter 4: it has the e to i change, like essen. Ich nehme, du nimmst, er nimmt. The thing you take is the object, so diesen is the form for a der-word. If you do not want it, you say nicht, and nicht goes to the end of the sentence, after the object.
cards.lead: You can describe clothes now. On this card: nehmen with dies- and nicht, so you can say which clothes you take and which you leave in the shop.

deeper.text: Nicht goes at the end when it says no to the whole sentence: Ich nehme dieses Hemd nicht. If you say no to one thing, you can use kein: Ich nehme keinen Gürtel. You know both from chapter 3. A yes/no question puts the verb first: Nimmst du diesen Mantel? You can answer ja or nein.

cards.title: Compare two: dieser ... aber dieser ...
cards.body: Compare two things with aber or und. After aber the second sentence starts as normal, with the subject first: Diese Jacke ist günstig, aber diese ist teuer. Dieser Mantel ist leicht, und dieser ist warm. Use dies- for both things.

examples.de: Diese Jacke ist günstig, aber diese ist teuer.
examples.en: This jacket is good value, but this one is expensive.

examples.de: Dieser Mantel ist leicht, und dieser ist warm.
examples.en: This coat is light, and this one is warm.

examples.de: Diese Schuhe sind eng, aber diese sind bequem.
examples.en: These shoes are tight, but these are comfortable.

steps: Say the first thing: Diese Jacke ist günstig
Add a comma and aber or und
Say the second thing: diese ist teuer
Together: Diese Jacke ist günstig, aber diese ist teuer.
cards.more: In a shop you often hold two things and compare them. Each thing gets its own short sentence, and a little joining word links them. Aber means but and shows a contrast, und means and. You know both from chapter 7, and they do not change the word order: the second sentence starts normally, with the subject, then the verb. The second diese or dieser stands alone, because everybody can see which thing you mean. This last card pulls the lesson together.
cards.lead: This is the last card of the lesson, and it pulls things together. You compare two things with aber and und, so you can explain why you take one jacket and leave the other.

deeper.text: The joining words aber and und stand outside the sentence, so the verb is still in part 2 of each half. A comma goes before aber, and often before und, too, when a full sentence follows. In English we say the same: this one is cheap, but this one is nice.

example.de: Dieser Schal ist billig, aber dieser ist hässlich.
example.en: This scarf is cheap, but this one is ugly.

lessons.title: mir, dir, ihm, ihr: pronouns in the dative
lessons.goal: Use the dative pronouns after mit, bei, von and zu, ask Wie geht es dir? and Wie geht es Ihnen?, and give, show and thank with the person first.

grammar.point: The dative pronouns are ich mir, du dir, er and es ihm, sie ihr, wir uns, ihr euch, sie (they) ihnen and Sie Ihnen. They stand after mit, bei, von, zu and aus, and with schenken, zeigen, geben, danken and gratulieren the person comes first.
grammar.oneLine: Ich schenke dir einen Pullover. Wie geht es Ihnen?

mistake.why: The person who gets the present is in the dative: dir, not dich. dich is only for the thing that your action hits, as in Ich rufe dich an.

terms.meaning: a small stand-in word for a person after mit, bei, von, zu, or when the person gets something: mir, dir, ihm, ihr
with schenken, zeigen and geben the person comes before the thing

cards.title: Before we start: with me, for you, to him
cards.body: Think of a birthday: you give a present, you say thank you, you ask how someone is. For all of this you need small words like mir, dir and ihm. You already know mit dem Chef (the dative) and mich, dich, ihn. Today those little words get a new form for the person who receives.

examples.why: You know this: mit + dative (chapter 7, lesson 3).
You know this: dich is the accusative pronoun (chapter 6, lesson 7).
New today: after mit the pronoun is dir, not dich.

steps: You already know: mit dem Chef, bei der Freundin (the dative, chapter 7) and mich, dich, ihn (chapter 6)
New today: mir, dir, ihm, ihr, uns, euch, ihnen, Ihnen, and the person-first order
By the end you can: say mit mir, bei dir, Wie geht es Ihnen? and Ich schenke dir einen Pullover
cards.more: Imagine two small words for the same person. When you call someone, you say dich: the person is the thing your action hits. When you give something to someone, or go with someone, you say dir: the person is the one who gets it or joins in. Mich becomes mir, dich becomes dir. A few pronouns stay the same, and you will see exactly which ones. You also learn to give, show, thank and congratulate, with the person first.

cards.title: The dative you know: a pronoun can take its place
cards.body: After mit, bei, von, zu and aus you already use the dative: mit dem Bus, bei der Freundin, von dem Chef. A pronoun can stand in for the whole noun phrase. Then the article disappears and one small word is left: mit dem Chef becomes mit ihm.

examples.en: Ben lives at the friend's place.
examples.why: bei + der Freundin: dative, you know this.
der Freundin is replaced by one word: ihr.
mit dem Chef becomes mit ihm.

cards.more: A pronoun is a stand-in. Instead of saying the long phrase again and again, you say one small word. Look at a team photo: the boss is in the picture, and later you only point and say him. In German the stand-in after mit, bei, von, zu or aus is a special dative word. For the boss, a das-word thing or a man, it is ihm. For a woman it is ihr. You keep the same five little words in front: mit, bei, von, zu, aus.
cards.lead: You have just met the idea of a stand-in word. Now we look at the five small words after the preposition, because they are the same in every sentence.

deeper.text: The preposition stays exactly where it is. Only the noun phrase after it is swapped for a pronoun. So the sentence keeps its shape: subject, verb, preposition, dative. If you can say the sentence with a noun, you can say it with a pronoun.

cards.title: Pronouns in the dative: the table
cards.body: Here are all the dative pronouns next to the nominative and the accusative you know. Look at the last column: ich becomes mir, du becomes dir, er and es become ihm, sie becomes ihr. Wir and ihr are special: uns and euch are the same in the accusative and the dative.

examples.why: ich → mir (the accusative would be mich).
er → ihm.
sie → ihr.

cards.more: Think of three columns: who does it, who gets hit, who gets it. Ich, mich, mir. Du, dich, dir. Er, ihn, ihm. Es, es, ihm. Sie, sie, ihr. Wir, uns, uns. Ihr, euch, euch. Sie (they), sie, ihnen. Sie (polite), Sie, Ihnen. Only two rows have the same word in the second and third column: uns and euch. Say the table out loud a few times, and the new column will soon feel as natural as the old two.
cards.lead: In the last card you saw that one small word can replace a noun phrase. This card gives you all the small words in one table, so you can look up any of them.

deeper.text: The dative forms of er and es are the same: ihm. The dative of sie (she) is ihr, and the dative of sie (they) is ihnen. Learn the polite form with a capital letter: Ihnen. A capital letter always means polite, and it sits in the middle of a sentence too.

cards.title: After mit, bei, von, zu, aus: use the table
cards.body: Use the table after the five dative words: mit mir, bei dir, von ihm, zu ihr, mit ihnen. One small warning: with a noun you say zum and zur, but with a pronoun you say only zu: zu mir, zu dir. There is no zum or zur in front of a pronoun.

examples.why: zu + pronoun: zu ihm, never zum ihm.
wir → uns, after mit.

examples.en: The present is from you all.
examples.why: ihr → euch, after von.

cards.more: Five little words open the door to the dative: mit, bei, von, zu, aus. Whatever follows them has to be in the dative, whether it is a noun or a pronoun. The table is your key: pick the person, find the dative, say it. With zu there is one trick. A noun uses zum or zur, because zu and dem melt together. A pronoun has no article, so nothing melts: zu mir, zu dir, zu ihm.
cards.lead: Now that you have the table, it is time to use it. This card shows the five prepositions with different pronouns, plus one small rule about zu.

deeper.text: The preposition is a signal: after mit, bei, von, zu or aus a dative comes next, so you never have to think about the verb. Watch bei: bei mir, bei dir means at my place, at your place. Germans use it all the time to plan a visit: Kommst du zu mir? Nein, wir sind heute bei dir.

example.en: We are at your place today.

cards.title: Wie geht es dir? Wie geht es Ihnen?
cards.body: To ask how someone is, you use geht es and the dative: Wie geht es dir? to a friend, Wie geht es Ihnen? to a stranger, Wie geht es euch? to several friends. To answer, put mir first: Mir geht es gut. It sounds like a chunk, so learn all of it as a whole.

examples.why: dir: you ask a friend (du).

examples.de: Wie geht es Ihnen, Frau Weber?
examples.why: Ihnen: the polite form, with a capital letter.
The answer starts with mir. The verb stays in position 2.

cards.more: You know Wie geht's? from the very first chapter. Now you see what is hiding inside: es geht dir, it goes to you. Everyone in the conversation is in the dative: dir for a friend, Ihnen for a stranger, euch for a group, mir for yourself. If you put mir first in the answer, geht es comes second, because the verb always sits in position 2. Greet your teacher with Ihnen and your friend with dir.
cards.lead: You can now use the pronouns after small words. Here is one of the most useful sentences in German, and it contains a dative pronoun too.

deeper.text: To say how someone else is, you use a name or er and sie: Wie geht es Ben? Es geht ihm gut. The names do not change in the dative, only the pronouns do. So you ask Wie geht es Ben? but you answer Ihm geht es gut.

cards.title: Give and show: the person comes first
cards.body: With schenken (to give as a present), zeigen (to show) and geben (to give) there are two objects: the person and the thing. The person is in the dative and comes first, the thing is in the accusative and comes second: Ich schenke dir einen Pullover. erklären, leihen and empfehlen work the same way.

examples.en: I give you a sweater as a present.
examples.why: Person first (dir), thing second (einen Pullover).
ihm = him, die Jacke = what is shown.
geben: the same order as schenken and zeigen.

cards.more: Imagine handing over a gift: first you look at the person, then you put the gift in their hand. German does exactly the same: the person first, then the thing. So the order is subject, verb, person, thing. The person is in the dative (dir, ihm, ihr), the thing is in the accusative. If the person is a name, the name stays the same: Ich zeige Ben das Hemd. Only pronouns change in the dative, so be careful with them.
cards.lead: Pronouns now sit after prepositions. A second big place for the dative is a verb with two objects. This card shows how the person and the thing line up.

deeper.text: English often needs the word to: I give the book to you. German needs no extra word, because the dative pronoun already says to you. geben and empfehlen change their vowel for du and er, like essen: du gibst, er gibt, er empfiehlt. leihen and erklären stay regular: er leiht, er erklärt.

cards.title: ihr, Ihr, ihnen, Ihnen: spot the difference
cards.body: Four look-alikes: ihr as a subject means you all (Kommt ihr?), and ihr as a dative means to her (Ich zeige ihr die Jacke). Ihnen with a small i means to them, and with a capital I it is polite: to you, Frau Weber. The verb and the sense tell you which one it is.

examples.why: ihr as subject: the verb ends in -t (kommt).
ihr as dative: the person who gets it.

examples.de: Ich zeige Ihnen die Jacke, Frau Weber.
examples.en: I show you the jacket, Frau Weber.
examples.why: Ihnen with a capital letter: polite you.

cards.more: These four words are like twins who dress alike. Ask two questions. First: is there a verb with -t right after it, like kommt ihr? Then it is you all, the subject. Second: who is meant? Is it one woman? Then it is ihr. Is it a group of people you talk about? Then ihnen with a small letter. Do you talk to a stranger and say Sie? Then Ihnen with a capital I. The capital letter in the middle of a sentence is the clue.
cards.lead: The table showed ihr, ihnen and Ihnen, and they look very much alike. This card puts them side by side, so you can tell them apart in a second.

deeper.text: A small trick helps with ihr. Change the sentence to du and the verb to -st: if it still works as a question to one person (Kommst du morgen?), then ihr was the you-all subject. Change ihr to ihm for a man: if it still works (Ich zeige ihm die Jacke), then ihr was the dative for a woman. The place in the sentence decides the meaning.

cards.title: Thank and congratulate: danken, gratulieren
cards.body: Two more verbs take a person in the dative: danken (to thank) and gratulieren (to congratulate). You say Ich danke dir and Ich gratuliere dir. On a birthday you add zum Geburtstag, a chunk. To thank someone in general, say Vielen Dank!

examples.why: danken + dative: dir, not dich.

examples.en: I congratulate you on your birthday.
examples.why: zum Geburtstag: learn it as a chunk (zu + dem).
dankt: er/sie/es ends in -t.

rows: I congratulate you on your birthday.

cards.more: Saying thank you is also a kind of giving, so the person is in the dative. Ich danke dir, Ich danke Ihnen, Ich danke euch. The same goes for congratulating: you give someone your good wishes, so you say Ich gratuliere dir. The little chunk zum Geburtstag means on the birthday. You know zum from chapter 7 as zu plus dem, and here you simply use it as a ready-made piece of the sentence.
cards.lead: You know how to give and show. Two more verbs also carry the person in the dative: thanking and congratulating, the best words for a party.

deeper.text: Vielen Dank! is a ready phrase: it means thank you very much. You can add the person with an extra sentence: Vielen Dank! Ich danke Ihnen. Both together sound friendly and polite, for example when a shop assistant has helped you or a friend has given you a present.

example.en: Thank you very much, Herr Ali!

lessons.title: gefallen: Die Jacke gefällt mir
lessons.goal: Say what you like with gefallen, ask Gefällt dir ...? and Wie gefällt Ihnen ...?, and give opinions about clothes.

grammar.point: With gefallen the thing is the subject and the person is in the dative: Die Jacke gefällt mir. One thing takes gefällt, several things take gefallen.
grammar.oneLine: Die Jacke gefällt mir. Die Schuhe gefallen mir.

mistake.why: The jacket is the one that pleases, so it is the subject. You are the person who likes it, so you are in the dative: mir.

terms.meaning: a verb whose person is in the dative, like gefallen: Die Jacke gefällt mir
the word that does the verb: with gefallen it is the thing that pleases

cards.title: Before we start: do you like it?
cards.body: In a shop, in a flat, at a party: people ask Do you like it? You already say Ich mag Käse and Ich finde das Zimmer schön. Today comes the most natural German way: Die Jacke gefällt mir. The jacket is the subject, and you, the person, are the small dative word mir from lesson 4.

examples.why: You know this: mögen + object (chapter 4, lesson 5).

examples.en: I think the room is nice.
examples.why: You know this: finden + object + adjective (chapter 9, lesson 8).
New today: the jacket pleases me. mir comes from lesson 4.

steps: You already know: Ich mag Käse (chapter 4), Ich finde das Zimmer schön (chapter 9), and mir, dir, ihm, ihr (lesson 4)
New today: Die Jacke gefällt mir, the thing is the subject and the person is in the dative
By the end you can: say Der Mantel gefällt mir, ask Gefällt dir das Kleid? and give an opinion
cards.more: In English you say I like the jacket, and you are the one who does it. In German there is a second way: the jacket does something to you. It pleases you. So the jacket is the subject, the verb is gefällt, and you are the person who gets the pleasure: mir. You already know mir from lesson 4, so there is nothing new to learn about it. It is the same idea as Ich schenke dir etwas, only turned around.

cards.title: gefallen: the thing does the pleasing
cards.body: gefallen means to please. The thing that pleases is the subject, and the person who likes it is in the dative: Die Jacke gefällt mir, word for word the jacket pleases me. It means the same as Ich mag die Jacke, but the sentence is built the other way round.

examples.why: Die Jacke is the subject; mir is the person.
dir: the person who likes it.
ihr: she, in the dative.

cards.more: Picture a jacket in a shop window. It looks at you and says: do I please you? The jacket is the active one, so the jacket is the subject. You are the one it pleases, so you are in the dative: mir. That is why the word for the person is so short and always comes after the verb: gefällt mir. The thing stays in front. If you want to say I like it, say it with the thing first: Die Jacke gefällt mir.
cards.lead: The introduction showed you the new building plan. This card puts the pieces side by side, so you see which word is the subject and which one is the person.

deeper.text: English has two ways to say it as well: I like the jacket and The jacket pleases me. German uses the second way very often, and it never says Ich gefalle for a thing you like. Remember: the thing is always the subject, and you are always in the dative.

cards.title: gefällt or gefallen? Look at the thing
cards.body: The verb agrees with the thing, not with the person. One thing: gefällt. Several things: gefallen. Learn them as two chunks together with mir or dir: Die Jacke gefällt mir, Die Schuhe gefallen mir. Jeans is a plural word, so you say Die Jeans gefallen mir.

examples.why: One thing (das Hemd): gefällt.
More than one (die Schuhe): gefallen.
Die Jeans is plural, so gefallen.

cards.more: Count what pleases you. One thing, one jacket: gefällt. Two shoes, many things: gefallen. The verb follows the thing, never the person. The person only changes the little word after it: mir, dir, ihm, ihr. You may notice the a becomes ä in gefällt, just like fahren becomes fährt. For now you do not need a whole table. Learn two ready pieces, gefällt mir and gefallen mir, and use them.
cards.lead: You know that the thing pleases the person. Now a small question: does the verb end in -t or -en? The answer depends on the thing, as this card shows.

deeper.text: The verb always matches the thing that pleases. If you say Die Jeans gefallen mir, the word Jeans decides: it is plural. If you ask Welcher Pullover gefällt dir?, the pullover decides: it is one thing. The little word mir or dir never changes the verb.

cards.title: Ask: Gefällt dir ...? Wie gefällt Ihnen ...?
cards.body: To ask a yes-or-no question, put the verb first: Gefällt dir der Pullover? To ask how someone likes it, start with Wie: Wie gefällt Ihnen das Kleid? You answer with er, sie or es for the thing: Ja, er gefällt mir. Nein, er gefällt mir nicht.

examples.why: Yes-no question: the verb is first.

examples.en: How do you like the dress?
examples.why: Wie + verb in position 2; Ihnen is polite.
er stands for der Pullover.

cards.more: The questions follow the rules you know. A question without a question word puts the verb first: Gefällt dir der Pullover? A question with Wie keeps the verb in position 2: Wie gefällt dir der Pullover? In the answer, a small stand-in word replaces the thing: er for a der-word, sie for a die-word, es for a das-word. For several things you use sie and gefallen: Ja, sie gefallen mir. You also see that nicht comes at the end: er gefällt mir nicht.
cards.lead: You can say what pleases you. Next, you want to ask others, in shops, with friends and with strangers. This card shows both kinds of questions and the short answers.

deeper.text: In the answer, er, sie and es are stand-in words for the thing, and they are in the nominative, because the thing is the subject. So you say Ja, sie gefällt mir about a jacket, and Ja, sie gefallen mir about shoes. The verb follows the thing, as before.

cards.title: How much? sehr gut, gut, nicht, gar nicht
cards.body: Show how much you like something with a short word: sehr gut (very much), gut, nicht so gut, nicht. The word nicht stands at the end: Der Pullover gefällt mir nicht. For a strong no, use the chunk gar nicht: Die Schuhe gefallen mir gar nicht.

examples.de: Das Kleid gefällt mir sehr gut.
examples.en: I like the dress very much.
examples.why: sehr gut at the end of the sentence.

examples.en: I do not like the sweater.
examples.why: nicht at the end, as in chapter 3.

examples.de: Die Schuhe gefallen mir gar nicht.
examples.en: I do not like the shoes at all.
examples.why: gar nicht: a strong no. Learn it as one chunk.

rows: Der Mantel gefällt mir sehr gut.
Die Hose gefällt mir nicht so gut.
Die Schuhe gefallen mir gar nicht.

cards.more: Think of a ladder with four steps. At the top: sehr gut, I love it. Then gut, then nicht so gut, and at the bottom: gar nicht, not at all. Each answer is a small word or two at the end of the sentence, after mir. You know sehr and nicht from chapter 3. The only new piece is gar nicht, which means not at all. You do not need to take it apart: use it as a ready piece when you really dislike something.
cards.lead: Now you can ask and answer. Opinions come in strengths, from very much to not at all. This card gives you a few ready words to put at the end of the sentence.

deeper.text: In real talk Germans often answer with the strength word alone: Gefällt dir die Jacke? Sehr gut! For a polite doubt they say Na ja, which sounds like well, hmm. Na ja, nicht so gut is softer than a plain nicht. Gar nicht is strong, so use it with friends, not with a shop assistant.

example.de: Na ja, die Jacke gefällt mir nicht so gut.
example.en: Well, I do not really like the jacket.

cards.title: Three ways to say I like it
cards.body: You now have three ways to say you like something. With mögen the person is the subject. With finden the person is the subject too, and you add an adjective. With gefallen the thing is the subject and the person is in the dative. All three are correct, and all three are everyday German.

examples.why: mögen: Ich is the subject, the trousers are the object.

examples.en: I think these trousers are nice.
examples.why: finden: the object gets an adjective.
gefallen: the trousers are the subject, mir is the dative.

cards.more: Three roads lead to the same place. On the first two roads you are the driver: Ich mag, Ich finde. On the third road the jacket drives and you sit in the back: Die Jacke gefällt mir. Look at the colours of the example sentences: with mögen and finden, ich is the subject. With gefallen, the thing is the subject and mir is the dative. If you mix them up, you get the typical mistake: Ich gefalle die Jacke.
cards.lead: You can choose how strong the opinion is. A last overview helps you not to mix up the three structures. Look at who is the subject in each one.

deeper.text: Finden is the only one of the three with an adjective: Ich finde die Hose schön. The adjective comes at the end and does not take an ending. With gefallen you can add a small word instead: Die Hose gefällt mir sehr gut. Both sentences say the same thing in different words.

example.en: I think the coat is nice.

cards.title: Opinion words: hübsch, schick, cool, komisch
cards.body: Four new words help you say what you think: hübsch (pretty), schick (smart, stylish), cool and komisch (strange, funny). Use them after sein or finden, with no ending: Das Kleid ist hübsch. Ich finde den Rock komisch. If someone agrees, you say Das finde ich auch.

examples.why: sein + adjective, no ending.

examples.en: I think the skirt is strange.
examples.why: finden + object + adjective: still no ending.
A short reaction. Das stands first, the verb is second.

cards.more: Four words and many opinions. Hübsch is a friendly one, schick sounds elegant, cool is the same as in English, and komisch is a little tricky: it means strange and also funny, so listen to the tone. You use them like all adjectives after sein or finden, at the end of the sentence, with no ending. When your friend says an opinion, you can reply with Wirklich? to be surprised, or Das finde ich auch to agree.
cards.lead: You can already say whether you like something. Now you add colour to the opinion, with four useful words for clothes and people.

deeper.text: Das finde ich auch is a ready reaction: it means I think so too. Das stands in position 1, then the verb finde, then ich. The word order looks turned around, but the verb is still in position 2, as always. Learn it whole, and you can use it in every conversation.

cards.title: Style and pattern: Stil, Muster, Mode
cards.body: Three more words belong to clothes: der Stil (style), das Muster (pattern) and die Mode (fashion). They work like all other nouns: Dieser Stil gefällt mir. Dieses Muster gefällt mir nicht. Die Mode in Berlin ist cool. The plural of Stil is Stile; Muster stays Muster.

examples.why: dieser Stil: you know dieser from lesson 3.

examples.en: I do not like this pattern.
examples.why: das Muster: dieses. nicht at the end.

examples.de: Die Mode in Berlin ist cool.
examples.en: The fashion in Berlin is cool.
examples.why: die Mode: usually no plural.

rows: Die Mode in Berlin ist cool.

cards.more: These three words help you talk about taste. Der Stil is the way something looks, like sporty or smart. Das Muster is what you see on a shirt: stripes, dots, flowers. Die Mode is what everybody wears right now. All three behave like the clothes you know: they have an article and they can be the subject of gefällt. And you have dieser, diese, dieses from lesson 3 to point at them.
cards.lead: You have the verb and the opinion words. The last card gives you three nouns for talking about taste, and you can use them as subjects of gefällt.

deeper.text: Mode usually has no plural, because it means fashion in general. Stil has a plural, die Stile, when you talk about different styles. Muster does not change: das Muster, die Muster. When in doubt about a new noun, look at its plural in a dictionary and learn it with the article.

example.de: Die Stile in Berlin sind cool.
example.en: The styles in Berlin are cool.

lessons.title: stehen, passen, aussehen: compliments and fit
lessons.goal: Pay and take compliments with stehen, say how something fits with passen and what goes with what with passt zu, and say how you look with aussehen.

grammar.point: stehen (it suits you) and passen (it fits you) also take the person in the dative: Das Kleid steht dir gut. Die Hose passt mir. With zu, passen means to go with: Die Schuhe passen zum Kleid.
grammar.oneLine: Das Kleid steht dir gut. Die Hose passt mir.

mistake.why: passen takes the dative, so you say mir, not mich. The trousers are the subject, you are the person who gets the fit.

terms.meaning: to go with: the second thing is in the dative (zum, zur)
a verb that splits: sehen in position 2 and aus at the end, as in Du siehst gut aus

cards.title: Before we start: that looks great on you!
cards.body: In a shop you try something on, and a friend says: Das steht dir gut! Two verbs you already know get a new job today: stehen, which you know from the lamp on the table, and passen. Both take the person in the dative, exactly like gefallen in lesson 5.

examples.de: Die Lampe steht auf dem Tisch.
examples.en: The lamp stands on the table.
examples.why: You know this: stehen = stand upright (chapter 9, lesson 5).
You know this: the thing is the subject, the person is the dative (lesson 5).
New today: stehen also means to suit, with a dative person.

steps: You already know: Die Lampe steht auf dem Tisch (chapter 9) and Die Jacke gefällt mir (lesson 5)
New today: stehen = to suit, passen = to fit, passen zu = to go with, aussehen = to look
By the end you can: say Das steht dir gut, Die Hose passt mir and Du siehst gut aus
cards.more: Words in every language can have a second life. The German stehen means to stand: the lamp stands on the table. But clothes can stand on you as well, and then it means that they suit you. Passen means that something fits: the right size, or a good match. In both cases the pattern is the one from lesson 5. The thing is the subject, and you are the dative: mir, dir, ihm, ihr. So you already know the grammar. You only add two meanings.

cards.title: stehen: it suits you
cards.body: When clothes look good on someone, German says that they stand on them: Das Kleid steht dir gut. The clothes are the subject, and the person is in the dative. The old meaning, Die Lampe steht auf dem Tisch, stays. You see which meaning is meant from the sentence.

examples.why: The dress is the subject; dir is the person.

examples.en: The shirt does not suit him.
examples.why: nicht at the end.

examples.de: Der Rock steht ihr sehr gut.
examples.en: The skirt suits her very much.
examples.why: ihr: she, in the dative.

rows: Die Lampe steht auf dem Tisch.

cards.more: Imagine a statue in a park. The statue stands. Now imagine a person in a shop mirror, and the dress stands on them like on a statue: it looks good on them. That is the picture behind Das Kleid steht dir gut. There are two meanings, but the grammar is the same as in lesson 5: the thing is the subject, the person is the dative, and gut or nicht stands at the end. If the sentence has a person in the dative and a piece of clothing, you can be sure it means to suit.
cards.lead: The introduction gave you the idea. Now the first of the new verbs: stehen with the meaning that clothes have on a person.

deeper.text: If you want to know whether stehen means stand or suit, look for the dative person and the clothes. Die Schuhe stehen vor der Tür means the shoes stand in front of the door. Die Schuhe stehen dir gut means they suit you. The place word or the dative word tells you which one it is.

cards.title: Blau steht dir: colours as nouns
cards.body: When the colour itself is the subject, it works as a noun: Blau steht dir. A sentence start always has a capital, but a noun keeps it in the middle too: Dir steht Blau gut. After sein the colour stays small: Die Jacke ist blau. There is no article and no ending.

examples.why: Blau at the start has a capital letter.
sehr gut at the end, as in lesson 5.
The colour is the subject; mir is the person.

cards.more: Colours play two roles. After sein the colour describes a thing, and it is a small word: Die Jacke ist blau. As the subject the colour is a thing itself, the idea blue. It is a noun, so it keeps its capital letter even in the middle of a sentence: Blau steht dir. Dir steht Blau gut. Think of a painter who says: blue looks good on you. There is no der, die or das before it. The same rule works for all colours you know: Rot, Blau, Grün, Gelb, Schwarz, Weiß, Braun, Grau.
cards.lead: You know that clothes can suit you. Colours can suit you too, and German writes them in a special way when they start the sentence.

deeper.text: The colour is the subject here, so the verb is the third-person form: steht. Even when you talk about a colour you cannot see, the verb is steht, never stehen. If you say two colours, the verb changes: Schwarz und Weiß stehen dir gut. Two colours are more than one thing.

cards.title: passen: it fits
cards.body: Passen means to fit, and it also takes the person in the dative: Die Hose passt mir. Die Jacke passt dir gut. Add nicht for a no: Die Hose passt mir nicht. For several things, use passen: Die Schuhe passen mir. Say why with zu groß (too big), zu klein (too small), locker (loose), or genau richtig (just right).

examples.en: The trousers do not fit me.
examples.why: The trousers are the subject; mir is the person.
More than one thing: passen.

examples.de: Die Hose passt mir nicht, sie ist zu klein.
examples.en: The trousers do not fit me, they are too small.
examples.why: Two short sentences with a comma. zu klein: too small.

rows: Der Mantel passt dir genau richtig.

cards.more: Passen is like gefallen in size: the clothes are the subject, the person is the dative. It answers the question: is it the right size? A bad fit has a reason, and you give it with a second short sentence: zu groß, zu klein, zu eng, sie ist zu lang. A good fit is genau richtig, exactly right. The word locker means loose and is the opposite of eng, tight. Plural things need passen, like gefallen: Die Schuhe passen mir.
cards.lead: You can say that something suits you. Now you say whether it fits. This card shows passen with the person in the dative, and the words for too big and too small.

deeper.text: The little word zu in zu klein is the same word you know from chapter 3: too. It stands in front of the adjective. zu klein means too small, and zu eng means too tight. But zu is also a preposition (zu mir): the meaning comes from the place in the sentence.

example.de: Die Jacke passt dir genau richtig.
example.en: The jacket fits you just right.

cards.title: passt zu: it goes with
cards.body: Passen has a second meaning with zu: to go with. The thing it goes with is in the dative: Der Gürtel passt zur Hose. Die Schuhe passen zum Kleid. You use only two forms: zum for der-words and das-words, zur for die-words. They are zu dem and zu der melted together.

examples.en: The belt goes with the trousers.
examples.why: die Hose: zu der melts to zur.

examples.en: The shoes go with the dress.
examples.why: das Kleid: zu dem melts to zum.

examples.en: The scarf goes with the coat.
examples.why: der Mantel: zu dem melts to zum.

cards.more: Think of two things that look good together, like a belt and trousers. German says the belt fits to the trousers: Der Gürtel passt zur Hose. After zu the dative comes, which you know from chapter 7. With this verb you only need two forms. For der-words and das-words, zu dem melts together to zum. For die-words, zu der melts together to zur. You already used zum with Geburtstag in lesson 4: zum Geburtstag.
cards.lead: You know passen for the fit on a person. The same verb can say that two things match, and then it is followed by zu and the dative.

deeper.text: The first thing is the subject and decides the verb, the second thing comes after zu. So the verb follows the first thing only: Der Gürtel passt zur Hose, but Die Schuhe passen zum Kleid. The word after zu has no influence on the verb. With the plural, the form is zu den and an n on the noun. For now, you only need zum and zur.

example.en: The sweater goes with the trousers.

cards.title: gefallen, stehen, passen side by side
cards.body: All three verbs work the same way: the thing is the subject, the person is in the dative, and the person sits after the verb. Gefallen says you like it, stehen says it suits you, passen says it fits. In questions they start with welch- as the subject: Welches Hemd steht dir? Welche Hose passt dir?

examples.why: welches: the shirt is the subject.
welche: die Hose, the subject.
welcher: the coat is the subject, so nominative.

cards.more: Three verbs, one pattern. The thing comes first and does the verb, the person comes after it in the dative. If you remember one sentence, remember this one: the thing is the subject. Then you cannot say Ich passe die Hose. In questions with welch- you also use the thing as a subject, so welch- is in the nominative: Welches Hemd steht dir? Welche Hose passt dir? Welcher Mantel gefällt dir? Only the end of the verb changes with the thing.
cards.lead: You now know three verbs with the same pattern. This card puts them in one table and shows them in questions with welch-, which you know from lesson 2.

deeper.text: In these questions welch- is in the nominative, because the thing is the subject. That means welcher for der-words, not welchen: Welcher Mantel passt dir? You use welchen only when the thing is the object, as in Welchen Mantel nimmst du? With a dative verb, the thing is never the object.

cards.title: aussehen: you look good
cards.body: Aussehen means to look. It is a separable verb, like anrufen: sehen goes in position 2 and aus goes to the end. Du siehst gut aus. Das sieht toll aus. Sehen has an e that changes to ie for du and er, sie, es: du siehst, er sieht. Here the person is the subject, not a dative.

examples.why: du siehst: e becomes ie, aus goes to the end.
Das sieht ... aus: the verb is split in two.
The time word comes after the verb; aus stays at the end.

cards.more: Aussehen is a verb with two parts. The main part, sehen, takes position 2 and is conjugated. The second part, aus, jumps to the end, like in Ich rufe dich an. You know that the e of sehen changes to ie for du and er, sie, es from chapter 2: du siehst, er sieht. Here you do not need the dative: Du siehst gut aus has du as subject. If you want to say how someone looks, put an adjective between: gut, toll, schick.
cards.lead: The three dative verbs are in place. One more useful verb for compliments is aussehen, and it has a different build: the person is the subject, and the verb is split.

deeper.text: Aussehen follows the rule for all separable verbs: the first part is conjugated and in position 2, the prefix goes to the end. Wir sehen heute schick aus. With a modal verb it stays together at the end: Ich möchte gut aussehen. For now, learn the split form with sehen and aus, as in the examples.

cards.title: Give and take a compliment
cards.body: Now put it all together. A compliment: Das steht dir gut! Du siehst gut aus! The answer: Danke! or Danke, wirklich? And when something is not right: Die Hose passt nicht, sie ist zu eng. Learn these as ready pieces. A Kompliment (plural: Komplimente) is always welcome, and perfekt is the best answer.

examples.why: A compliment: dir, the dative.
The answer, with mir.
perfekt: a new word, no ending.

rows: Die Hose passt nicht, sie ist zu eng.
Schade! Die Jacke steht dir gut.

cards.more: Think of a short dialogue as a small play. One person gives a compliment, the other one answers, and both are happy. The pieces are ready-made: Das steht dir gut! is the compliment. Danke, wirklich? shows you are surprised. Ja, perfekt! is the happy answer. If something is wrong, you say the problem plainly: Die Hose passt nicht, sie ist zu eng. Learn the pieces and you can play every shop scene.
cards.lead: You have every piece: stehen, passen, aussehen. This last card puts them into a short dialogue you can use in a shop, with a friend or at a party.

deeper.text: In German it is polite to answer a compliment with Danke, not to say no. If you do not agree, you can add a soft Wirklich? (you know it from lesson 5). Compliments for your friends use dir, and for a stranger like Frau Weber you use Ihnen: Das steht Ihnen gut, Frau Weber.
