lessons.title: helfen and gehören: in the clothes shop
lessons.goal: Take part in a shop dialogue (Kann ich Ihnen helfen?, size, colour, fit, price, pay) and say whose clothes they are.

grammar.point: helfen and gehören take the dative: Kann ich Ihnen helfen? Der Mantel gehört mir. Wem gehört das? The five dative verbs are gefallen, stehen, passen, helfen and gehören.
grammar.oneLine: Kann ich Ihnen helfen? Wem gehört der Mantel? Er gehört mir.

mistake.why: helfen takes the dative, so the polite word is Ihnen (or dir), not dich.

terms.meaning: the five verbs gefallen, stehen, passen, helfen and gehören: the person is in the dative
to whom? (the dative of wer): Wem gehört der Mantel?

cards.title: Before we start: Kann ich Ihnen helfen?
cards.body: In every clothes shop someone asks Kann ich Ihnen helfen? You already ask Haben Sie ...? in shops, and you know Ihnen from lesson 4. Today you learn why it is Ihnen and not Sie: helfen takes the dative. Then you walk through a whole shop visit, from the changing room to the till.

examples.why: You know this: Haben Sie ...? (chapter 4).
You know this: Ihnen is the polite dative (lesson 4).
New today: helfen takes the dative, so Ihnen.

steps: You already know: Haben Sie ...? (chapter 4), Können Sie bitte ...? (chapter 7) and Ihnen (lesson 4)
New today: helfen and gehören take the dative, plus the words of a shop visit
By the end you can: manage a short shop dialogue, from Kann ich Ihnen helfen? to the receipt
cards.more: Think of a helper in a shop. You do not hit the helper or take the helper, like a thing. You do something for the person. German marks that with the small dative words you already know: mir, dir, Ihnen. So helfen always comes with the dative. In this lesson you also learn a second dative verb, gehören, a few shop phrases and how to pay. Take it one card at a time.

cards.title: helfen: to help someone
cards.body: helfen changes e to i for du and er/sie/es, like essen. The person you help is in the dative: Ich helfe dir. Mira hilft ihm. A name in the dative does not change: Wir helfen Frau Weber.

examples.why: The person you help is in the dative: dir.
er/sie/es: e becomes i.
A name in the dative stays the same.

cards.more: Say it as two small pieces: helfen plus the person. Ich helfe dir. Mira hilft ihm. In English I help him looks like I see him. In German they are different: sehen takes ihn, but helfen takes ihm. So always ask yourself: do I do something to the person, or for the person? With helfen it is for. Then use mir, dir, ihm, ihr, uns, euch, ihnen or Ihnen.
cards.lead: In lesson 5 you met your first dative verbs. Now helfen joins them. On this card you learn its forms, with e becoming i, so you can say who helps whom.

deeper.text: English does not show the difference: help him and see him look the same. German does. sehen is about the person as a thing you see, so you say ihn. helfen is about doing something for the person, so you say ihm. Learn helfen together with the dative: helfen + dir.

cards.title: Kann ich Ihnen helfen?
cards.body: A salesperson asks: Kann ich Ihnen helfen? The modal kann is in part 2, helfen goes to the end, and Ihnen sits in the middle. You can answer Ja, ich suche eine Jacke. or just say Ich schaue nur. (I am just looking.) Learn Ich schaue nur as one piece.

examples.why: Modal in part 2, helfen at the end.
You ask for help: mir.
Learn it as one piece.

cards.more: You know the bracket from chapter 5: the modal comes second and the other verb waits at the end. Everything else goes in between. Kann ich Ihnen helfen: Ihnen sits between. In the shop you have two easy answers. If you want something, say Ja, ich suche ... and name it. If you do not, say Ich schaue nur and the salesperson leaves you alone.
cards.lead: You know the modal bracket from chapter 5. On this card it appears in the question every salesperson asks, so you can understand it and answer it in a shop.

deeper.text: When you are the customer, you turn the bracket around: Können Sie mir helfen? The dative word still sits between the two verb parts. You can add bitte to sound polite. If someone offers help, Ja, gern is a friendly answer.

cards.title: gehören: whose is it?
cards.body: gehören means to belong to. The owner is in the dative. Ask with wem (to whom?): Wem gehört der Mantel? Answer: Er gehört mir. One thing: gehört. Several things: gehören. A name stays the same: Die Schuhe gehören Ben.

examples.why: wem = to whom? (the dative of wer).
The owner is in the dative: mir.
More than one: gehören.

cards.more: Imagine a pile of clothes and a label on each one. Wem gehört die Jacke? means: who is the owner? The answer is a dative word, because the owner is the person who gets the thing: Sie gehört mir, Sie gehört Frau Weber. The verb agrees with the thing, not with the owner, so one jacket is gehört and two shoes are gehören.
cards.lead: helfen is not the only new dative verb in this lesson. Next you learn gehören, which tells you who owns something, so you can ask Wem gehört das? in a shop or at a party.

deeper.text: The verb agrees with the thing, like gefallen in lesson 5. If you ask about one thing, you say gehört. If you ask about several things, you say gehören. The owner after it does not change the verb at all: it can be mir, ihm or a name.

cards.title: Five dative verbs: your list
cards.body: You now know five verbs whose person is in the dative: gefallen, stehen, passen, helfen, gehören (plus danken and gratulieren from lesson 4). Verbs like essen and trinken are different: their thing is the accusative (Ich esse einen Apfel). Learn each dative verb together with mir: gefällt mir, steht mir, passt mir, hilft mir, gehört mir.

examples.why: gefallen: the person is in the dative.
stehen (suit): the person is in the dative.
essen is different: the thing is the accusative.

cards.more: Make a short list in your head, a tiny toolbox of five. gefallen, stehen, passen, helfen, gehören. When you use one of them, reach for mir, dir, ihm, ihr or Ihnen. Do not use mich or dich. Add danken and gratulieren from lesson 4. For verbs like essen, trinken or kaufen, the thing is the accusative. If you are unsure, remember these and treat everything else as normal.
cards.lead: You have met these verbs one by one. On this card you see all five together in one list, so you can learn each one with its small dative word and not mix them up with essen or trinken.

deeper.text: Careful: not every verb with a person takes the dative. fragen, besuchen and anrufen take the accusative: Ich frage dich, Ich besuche dich, Ich rufe dich an. Only the verbs on your list, plus danken and gratulieren, take mir and dir. One sentence can even have both: Ich frage dich, und dann helfe ich dir.

example.de: Ich frage dich, und dann helfe ich dir.
example.en: I ask you, and then I help you.

cards.title: At the shop: size, colour, fit
cards.body: Learn these as ready pieces. Welche Größe haben Sie? Ich habe Größe 40. Haben Sie das in Blau? The colour after in has a capital letter. If it is not right: Er ist zu klein. Er ist zu groß. To try something on: Möchten Sie die Jacke anprobieren? Wo ist die Umkleidekabine?

examples.why: Welche: the question word from lesson 2.

examples.en: Do you have that in blue?
examples.why: in + colour: a ready piece, capital letter.

examples.en: Would you like to try the jacket on?
examples.why: anprobieren is separable. With möchten it stays whole at the end.

rows: Welche Größe haben Sie? / Ich habe Größe 40.
Er ist zu klein. / Er ist zu groß.

cards.more: Think of a shop dialogue as a small play with fixed lines. The salesperson says: Welche Größe haben Sie? You answer with a number: Ich habe Größe 40. You ask for a colour: Haben Sie das in Blau? If something does not fit you say: zu klein or zu groß. With möchten, anprobieren stays in one piece at the end. Without möchten, the prefix goes to the end: Ich probiere die Hose an.
cards.lead: You know how to ask for help. On this card you learn the pieces you need inside the shop: sizes, colours, too big or too small, and the changing room.

deeper.text: German sizes are not English sizes. Women often wear 36, 38 or 40, men 48, 50 or 52, and shoes go from about 36 to 46. In the shop people also say Nummer instead of Größe: Ich habe Nummer 40. And many people just say die Kabine for the long word Umkleidekabine.

cards.title: Offers and price
cards.body: To ask the price: Was kostet die Jacke? A sale item is im Angebot (on offer, a ready piece). A discount is der Rabatt: Mit Rabatt kostet der Mantel 50 Euro. You can say Das ist zu teuer. or ask Ist das günstig? Günstig (good value) and billig (cheap) both mean a low price.

examples.why: Was kostet ...? asks for the price.
im Angebot: a ready piece.

examples.de: Mit Rabatt kostet der Mantel 50 Euro.
examples.en: With the discount the coat costs 50 euros.
examples.why: Mit Rabatt first, so kostet is part 2.

rows: With a discount it costs 50 euros.
Mit Rabatt kostet der Mantel 50 Euro.

cards.more: Prices are easy to ask for. You say Was kostet ... and name the thing. One thing: kostet. Several things: kosten. The salesperson answers with a number and Euro. If a sign says Angebot, the item is cheaper today. If the price is too high, say Das ist zu teuer. If you like it, ask Ist das günstig? and wait for the answer.
cards.lead: You can now ask for help and describe a size. This card gives you the words for money: price, sale and discount, so you can ask what something costs and say if it is too much.

deeper.text: When you ask about several things, the verb changes to kosten: Was kosten die Schuhe? The verb follows the thing, just as with gefallen and gehören. The answer then uses sind: Die Schuhe sind günstig. For one thing it is ist.

cards.title: At the till
cards.body: At the till (die Kasse) you can say Ich zahle bar (in cash) or Ich zahle mit der Karte (with the card). After mit comes the dative: mit der Karte. You can ask for a receipt: Ich brauche eine Quittung. Finish with Danke, schönen Tag! Read the whole shop dialogue below, line by line.

examples.why: bar: a ready piece.
mit + dative: der Karte.
brauchen + accusative: eine Quittung.

steps: Verkäuferin: Guten Tag! Kann ich Ihnen helfen?
Frau Weber: Ja, ich suche einen Mantel. Ich habe Größe 40.
Verkäuferin: Möchten Sie den Mantel anprobieren? Die Umkleidekabine ist dort.
Frau Weber: Er passt mir gut. Was kostet er?
Verkäuferin: Er kostet 80 Euro, aber er ist im Angebot.
Frau Weber: Ich zahle mit der Karte. Ich brauche eine Quittung.
Verkäuferin: Bitte schön. Danke, schönen Tag!
cards.more: The till is the last step of the shop dialogue. You say how you pay, you ask for a receipt if you need one, and you say thank you. Look at the dialogue as a chain: help, size, try on, price, pay. Each link is a sentence you already know. When you can say all of them in order, you can handle a real shop.
cards.lead: You now have every piece of a shop visit. This last card puts them in order: you pay, you ask for a receipt, and you read the whole dialogue between a customer and a salesperson.

deeper.text: A very common ending is Danke, schönen Tag! It means thank you, have a nice day. The salesperson often answers with Danke, gleichfalls! (the same to you). You can learn it as one piece, without any grammar. It is polite and short, and every shop assistant likes it.

lessons.title: In the department store: Wo finde ich ...?
lessons.goal: Read a store directory, find a department, ask for information, say which floor, and use welch- and dies- in the dative.

grammar.point: welch- and dies- follow the der-endings in the dative: welchem / welcher / welchem / welchen + n and diesem / dieser / diesem / diesen + n. Floors use in + dative: im ersten Stock.
grammar.oneLine: In welchem Stock ist die Kasse? Die Schuhabteilung ist im zweiten Stock.

mistake.wrong: In welcher Stock ist die Kasse?
mistake.right: In welchem Stock ist die Kasse?
mistake.why: Stock is masculine and in + wo? takes the dative, so the word is welchem.

terms.meaning: floor of a building: im ersten Stock = on the first floor
wo? = where (in + dative); wohin? = where to (in + accusative)

cards.title: Before we start: where is the shoe department?
cards.body: In a big Kaufhaus you need a map. You already ask Wo ist ...? and say in der Kantine (in + dative, chapter 7). Today you read a store directory, say the floor with im zweiten Stock, and learn welchem and diesem, the dative of welch- and dies-.

examples.why: You know this: Wo ist ...? (chapter 3).
You know this: in + dative answers wo? (chapter 7).

examples.de: Die Schuhabteilung ist im zweiten Stock.
examples.en: The shoe department is on the second floor.
examples.why: New today: im zweiten Stock.

steps: You already know: Wo ist ...? (chapter 3), in der Kantine (chapter 7) and the ordinals erste, zweite, dritte (chapter 6)
New today: floors (im zweiten Stock), departments, and welchem / diesem in the dative
By the end you can: read a directory, ask Wo finde ich die Schuhabteilung? and say which floor
cards.more: A department store is like a small town, stacked up in layers. Each layer is a floor, and each floor has its own shops. You do not walk around and guess. You read the directory by the entrance, find your word, read the number next to it and go there. In this lesson you get the words for the map, the questions to ask, and the endings you need to say which floor.

cards.title: Read the store directory
cards.body: A directory lists every floor and what you find there. Three steps: find your word, read the floor next to it, then find the stairs, the escalator or the lift. Erdgeschoss is the ground floor. The floors above are called 1. Stock, 2. Stock and so on.

examples.en: The information desk is on the ground floor.
examples.why: Im Erdgeschoss: a ready piece for the ground floor.

examples.de: Im zweiten Stock ist die Schuhabteilung.
examples.en: The shoe department is on the second floor.
examples.why: 2. Stock is read as zweiter Stock; after im it becomes zweiten.

examples.de: Im vierten Stock ist die Kinderabteilung.
examples.en: The children's department is on the fourth floor.
examples.why: The place comes first, then the verb.

cards.more: A directory is a little table. On the left you see the floor, on the right you see what is there. Put your finger on your word, then slide left to the floor. That is all. You do not need to understand every word. Only look for the one thing you want. Then ask yourself: stairs, escalator or lift? German shops show all three with signs.
cards.lead: You can already ask for help in a shop. Now you step into a big department store. This card shows you how to read the directory by the entrance so you can find any floor.

deeper.text: The directory says 2. Stock, but you read it aloud as zweiter Stock. In the sentence it becomes im zweiten Stock. Do not worry about the ending yet. You will see exactly why on the next cards. For now you can learn im ersten, im zweiten, im dritten and im vierten Stock as four ready pieces.

example.de: Im ersten Stock ist die Damenabteilung.
example.en: The women's department is on the first floor.

cards.title: Departments
cards.body: A department is an Abteilung, and every word that ends in -abteilung is a die-word. Damenabteilung is for women, Herrenabteilung for men, Kinderabteilung for children, Schuhabteilung for shoes. The department store itself is das Kaufhaus, plural die Kaufhäuser. After Ich suche the word die stays die.

examples.en: I am looking for the men's department.
examples.why: Accusative: die stays die.

examples.en: We are looking for the children's department.
examples.why: Wir: suchen.

examples.en: The department store is very big.
examples.why: das Kaufhaus, die Kaufhäuser.

cards.more: Learn the word Abteilung as a box with a label. The label says who it is for: Damen, Herren, Kinder, Schuh. All of them are die-words, because the box itself, die Abteilung, is a die-word. So you only need to learn one article. The plural adds -en: die Damenabteilungen. For the shop itself, remember das Kaufhaus and its plural die Kaufhäuser, with an umlaut.
cards.lead: You know how to read the directory. Now you learn the names of the departments themselves. All of them are die-words, so you only learn one article.

deeper.text: The first part tells you who the department is for, and the second part is always -abteilung. German makes long words by putting short words together: Schuh + Abteilung. The last part decides the article, so all of them are die. You will find many such words in Berlin: a Kaufhaus often has more than ten departments.

cards.title: Which floor? im ersten Stock
cards.body: Where is something? Use in + dative, as in chapter 7: in dem becomes im. The floor number is an ordinal (chapter 6) and after im it ends in -en: im ersten Stock, im zweiten, im dritten, im vierten. The ground floor is im Erdgeschoss. To go up, you say mit der Rolltreppe or mit dem Aufzug.

examples.de: Die Kasse ist im dritten Stock.
examples.en: The till is on the third floor.
examples.why: in + dem = im, then -en: dritten.
mit + dative: der Rolltreppe.
mit + dative: dem Aufzug.

rows: mit der Rolltreppe / mit dem Aufzug

cards.more: Stock is a der-word. Where is it? In dem Stock, which melts to im Stock. After dem the number word takes -en, just like in am dritten Mai (on the third of May) in chapter 6. So the pattern is always im + ordinal + -en + Stock. For the ground floor there is no number: im Erdgeschoss. You will not need any other floors in a normal shop.
cards.lead: You can read the directory. Now you say where something is. This card shows how in + dative and the ordinal come together: im ersten Stock, im zweiten Stock and so on.

deeper.text: Careful with floor numbers. In Germany the floor at street level is the Erdgeschoss, floor zero. The erste Stock is one floor up, which Americans call the second floor. So a sign with 3. Stock means three floors above the street. In the lift the Erdgeschoss button is often E or 0.

example.de: Der erste Stock ist über dem Erdgeschoss.
example.en: The first floor is above the ground floor.

cards.title: Ask: Wo finde ich ...?
cards.body: To find something, ask Entschuldigung, wo finde ich die Schuhabteilung? The verb finden stays in part 2 and takes the accusative (chapter 9). Someone answers Im zweiten Stock. You say Danke! You can also ask Wo ist der Ausgang? or Wo ist der Eingang?

examples.de: Entschuldigung, wo finde ich die Schuhabteilung?
examples.en: Excuse me, where do I find the shoe department?
examples.why: finden + accusative: die Schuhabteilung.
der Ausgang.
Plural: sind, die Eingänge.

rows: Entschuldigung, wo finde ich die Schuhabteilung?
Dort. Fahren Sie mit der Rolltreppe.

cards.more: Imagine you are lost between racks of clothes. You do not need a long speech. Start with Entschuldigung, then wo, then the verb right after it: wo finde ich, wo ist, wo sind. The thing you look for comes last. The answer you get is short too, often only the floor: Im zweiten Stock. Say Danke, and off you go. Three small lines, and you have found your department.
cards.lead: You can now say where something is. This card turns that into a question: you ask a person in the shop where to find a department, the entrance or the exit.

deeper.text: Ask with ist for one thing and sind for several. Ausgang and Eingang have an umlaut in the plural: die Ausgänge, die Eingänge. A big Kaufhaus often has more than one entrance, so you may need the plural when you ask.

example.en: Where do I find the escalator?

cards.title: Where to? Wohin: in den zweiten Stock
cards.body: Wo? asks about a place and takes the dative: im zweiten Stock, in der Damenabteilung. Wohin? asks about a direction and takes the accusative: in den zweiten Stock, in die Damenabteilung. Compared with the nominative, only der-words change: den. Die-words keep die.

examples.en: Mira is in the shoe department.
examples.why: wo? in + dative: der.

examples.en: I go to the women's department.
examples.why: wohin? in + accusative: die.

examples.de: Fahren Sie mit der Rolltreppe in den zweiten Stock.
examples.en: Take the escalator to the second floor.
examples.why: wohin? in + accusative: den zweiten Stock.

cards.more: Think of in as a door. If you are already inside, you ask wo and say im Stock or in der Abteilung. If you walk through the door, you ask wohin and say in den Stock or in die Abteilung. In the accusative only der-words change: in den Stock. The die-words keep die: in die Abteilung. You already did this with in der Kantine and in die Kantine in chapter 7.
cards.lead: You can say where something is. Now you say where you are going. This card shows the difference between wo and wohin, the dative and the accusative, in a store.

deeper.text: Here is a quick way to check. Look at the question. Wo? means you stay in one place, so you use the dative. Wohin? means you move, so you use the accusative. In both cases the word in stays the same. Only the article after it changes.

cards.title: welch- and dies- in the dative
cards.body: welch- (which) and dies- (this) take the der-endings from lesson 2. In the dative they are welchem / welcher / welchem / welchen and diesem / dieser / diesem / diesen. In the dative plural the noun also gets an extra -n: mit diesen Schuhen. In welchem Stock? In welcher Abteilung?

examples.de: In welchem Stock ist die Kasse?
examples.en: On which floor is the till?
examples.why: Stock is masculine: welchem.

examples.de: In welcher Abteilung finde ich Hosen?
examples.en: In which department do I find trousers?
examples.why: Abteilung is feminine: welcher.

examples.de: In diesem Geschäft arbeitet mein Bruder.
examples.en: My brother works in this shop.
examples.why: Geschäft is neuter: diesem.

cards.more: welch- and dies- are like a der-word in disguise. They follow the same endings. In the dative the pattern is dem, der, dem, den, and the endings follow: -em, -er, -em, -en. So dem Stock becomes welchem Stock, der Abteilung becomes welcher Abteilung, dem Geschäft becomes diesem Geschäft. In the plural, den Schuhen becomes diesen Schuhen, and the noun gets an extra n.
cards.lead: You know welch- and dies- from lessons 2 and 3 in the nominative and the accusative. This card adds the dative, so you can ask in welchem Stock and in welcher Abteilung.

deeper.text: Look at the article first. dem, der, dem, den. Then change only the ending of welch- or dies-. If the article is dem, you say welchem. If it is den, you say welchen. A plural dative noun also gets -n: den Schuhen. Nouns that already end in -n do not get a second one.

example.de: Mit diesen Schuhen gehe ich nach Hause.
example.en: I walk home in these shoes.

cards.title: Ask politely for information
cards.body: In a big store you need polite questions. Use Entschuldigung and Sie. Ask for help: Entschuldigung, können Sie mir bitte helfen? Ask for a size: Haben Sie diese Hose in Größe 38? Ask for the till: Wo ist die Kasse? The little dative word mir sits between the verbs.

examples.en: Excuse me, can you help me, please?
examples.why: Modal + mir + helfen.

examples.de: Haben Sie diese Hose in Größe 38?

Wo ist ...? is always polite enough with Entschuldigung.

rows: Entschuldigung, können Sie mir bitte helfen?
Haben Sie diese Hose in Größe 38?

cards.more: Polite shop language is a small set of building blocks. Start with Entschuldigung. Then choose a frame: Können Sie mir bitte helfen, Haben Sie ..., or Wo ist ... Then add the thing you want. You already know every part from the earlier cards: Sie, mir, bitte, Größe, Kasse. Put them together, and you can ask anything in a Kaufhaus.
cards.lead: This is the last card before the practice. You put everything together: help, size and place, in the polite frames you can use every day in a department store.

deeper.text: Entschuldigung is the short, everyday form. Entschuldigen Sie is a little more formal and very common with strangers. Natives also like to start with Ich suche: Ich suche die Kasse. It sounds softer than a direct question, and staff understand at once that you need help.

example.de: Entschuldigen Sie, ich suche die Kasse.
example.en: Excuse me, I am looking for the till.

lessons.title: My shopping day: the Perfekt with separable and inseparable verbs
lessons.goal: Tell a shopping day in the Perfekt, say Die Jacke hat mir gefallen, and hear the stress on prefix verbs.

grammar.point: Separable verbs put ge in the middle (eingekauft, umgetauscht, ausgesucht, zurückgegeben, ausgegeben); anprobieren has no ge because of -ieren; inseparable verbs have no ge (bekommen, verkauft, vergessen, bezahlt). Dative verbs in the Perfekt: Die Jacke hat mir gefallen.
grammar.oneLine: Ich habe eine Jacke ausgesucht und anprobiert. Die Jacke hat mir gefallen.

mistake.why: The participle goes to the very end, and the dative pronoun stays before it.

terms.meaning: a verb with a small word in front: einkaufen, bekommen
separable: the prefix can leave the verb (ein-, aus-, um-). Inseparable: it never leaves (be-, ver-)

cards.title: Before we start: tell me about your shopping day
cards.body: A friend asks: What did you buy? You can already tell a day in the Perfekt: Ich bin um sieben aufgestanden, Ich habe Pizza bestellt (chapter 10). Today you tell a shopping day with new verbs like ausgesucht, umgetauscht and bekommen, and you learn which verbs get ge- and where the stress goes.

examples.why: You know this: ge goes in the middle (chapter 10, lesson 6).
You know this: be- verbs have no ge- (chapter 10, lesson 3).
New today: aus + ge + sucht = ausgesucht.

steps: You already know: the Perfekt bracket and aufgestanden, bestellt, bezahlt (chapter 10)
New today: the participles of shopping verbs, with ge- in the middle or no ge- at all, and the stress on these verbs
By the end you can: say Ich habe eine Jacke ausgesucht und anprobiert and tell a shopping day in order
cards.more: A shopping day is a little story: you looked, you chose, you tried on, you paid, maybe you exchanged something. German tells it in the Perfekt, with haben in part 2 and the participle at the end. The only tricky part is the participle of verbs with a small word in front, like ausgesucht or bekommen. Today you learn the simple rule: some get ge- in the middle, some get no ge- at all.

cards.title: The Perfekt bracket and the story order
cards.body: Review: haben is in part 2 and the participle goes to the very end: Ich habe eine Jacke gekauft. A shopping story goes in order: zuerst, dann, danach. After zuerst the verb stays in part 2, so haben comes before ich: Zuerst habe ich eingekauft.

examples.why: haben in part 2, participle last.
Time first: the verb stays in part 2.
One more step of the story.

cards.more: Think of a train with two special seats. The first seat, in part 2, belongs to haben. The last seat belongs to the participle. Everything else sits in between. When you start with zuerst, dann or danach, the time word takes the first seat of the sentence, and the subject steps behind haben. The train still has the same two special seats.
cards.lead: Before the new verbs, a short review. You already know the bracket from chapter 10. This card also shows how to put a shopping story in order with zuerst, dann and danach.

deeper.text: The participles on this card are all known from chapter 10. gekauft and bezahlt have the usual -t. eingekauft has ge in the middle, because ein- is a separable prefix. mitgebracht is separable too, with ge in the middle: mit + ge + bracht. gegeben is irregular and has ge at the front. Today you add more verbs to this list.

cards.title: Separable verbs: ge in the middle
cards.body: A separable verb has a small word in front that can stand alone: aus, um, zurück, ein, an. In the Perfekt, ge goes between the prefix and the stem: aussuchen, ausgesucht. Anprobieren is the one exception in the list: no ge, because verbs ending in -ieren never have one: anprobiert.

examples.why: um + ge + tauscht.
zurück + ge + geben (irregular, like gegeben).
an + probiert: no ge, because of -ieren.

steps: Find the prefix: aus-, um-, zurück-, ein-, an-
Put ge after the prefix: aus + ge
Add the stem + t (regular) or the stem + en (irregular)
cards.more: Take the verb apart like a toy. The prefix is the first block, the stem is the second. In the Perfekt you push a small ge between the blocks: um + ge + tauscht. Regular verbs end in -t. Irregular ones, like geben, end in -en: zurückgegeben. One block is special: anprobieren is built from an + probieren. Verbs ending in -ieren never take ge, so you get anprobiert.
cards.lead: You learned in chapter 10 that separable verbs put ge in the middle. This card gives you five shopping verbs that follow the same rule, and one that does not, anprobieren.

deeper.text: aussuchen and ausgeben look similar but they are different. aussuchen is regular: aus + ge + sucht. ausgeben is irregular like geben: aus + ge + geben. Check the plain verb. If you know gegeben, you know ausgegeben and zurückgegeben too. This is why one small list is enough.

example.en: Mira spent a lot of money.

cards.title: Inseparable verbs: no ge-
cards.body: Some prefixes never separate: be- and ver- are the ones you need today. Verbs with them have no ge- in the participle. bekommen stays bekommen. verkaufen becomes verkauft, bezahlen becomes bezahlt. vergessen stays vergessen. Nothing is added in front. Regular ones only add -t.

examples.why: bekommen: the infinitive and the participle are the same.

examples.de: Der Verkäufer hat die Jacke verkauft.
examples.why: ver- : no ge-, stem + t.
vergessen: irregular, same as the infinitive.

cards.more: Compare two verbs: einkaufen and bekommen. They both have a small word in front. But ein- is a word on its own, so it can leave the verb and go to the end: Ich kaufe ein. be- is only a syllable, so it can never leave the verb. That is why bekommen has no ge in the middle. The same is true for ver-: verkaufen, vergessen. Hear the stress: it is on the stem, not on be- or ver-.
cards.lead: The last card gave you verbs where ge goes in the middle. This card shows the opposite group: verbs that never get a ge, because the prefix is be- or ver-.

deeper.text: You have seen this group in chapter 10, with bezahlen and bestellen. Today bekommen, verkaufen and vergessen join it. Quick test: if the verb starts with be-, ver- or er-, do not add ge-. It is one of the easiest rules in the Perfekt. Many everyday verbs follow it.

cards.title: Dative verbs in the Perfekt
cards.body: The dative verbs use haben in the Perfekt. gefallen: the infinitive and the participle look the same. The ge- is already inside the verb, so nothing is added. passen becomes gepasst, gehören becomes gehört, helfen becomes geholfen (irregular, like gegeben). The dative pronoun stays before the participle.

examples.why: gefallen: no extra ge; mir stays before it.
passen: ge + pass + t.
helfen: geholfen, irregular.

cards.more: You learned the five dative verbs. They behave in the Perfekt just like other verbs: haben in part 2, the participle at the end. The only extra rule is this: the little dative word, mir or dir, sits between haben and the participle. So you say Die Jacke hat mir gefallen. Not hat gefallen mir. You can compare it with the Perfekt bracket from chapter 10: nothing is new, only the dative word is added.
cards.lead: You know the five dative verbs in the present. This card shows how they look in the Perfekt, so you can say Die Jacke hat mir gefallen and ask Wer hat dir geholfen?

deeper.text: Notice that gefallen and gehören look like they have ge- already, and they do: the ge- is part of the verb. So the participle of gefallen is gefallen, and gehört comes from gehören. You do not add another ge. Today you only need these four.

cards.title: Stress: prefix or stem?
cards.body: You can hear which kind of verb it is. In separable verbs the prefix gets the stress: UMtauschen, AUSgeben, AUSsuchen, EINkaufen (but -ieren wins: anproBIEren). In inseparable verbs the stem gets the stress: beKOMmen, verKAUfen, verGESsen, beZAHlen. Say each one aloud and clap on the stressed syllable.

examples.why: UM is the prefix: UMtauschen.
be- is never stressed: beKOMme.

examples.en: We spend a lot of money.
examples.why: AUS is the prefix: AUSgeben.

cards.more: Stress is the loud part of a word. Say Banane: you push the middle part. In German verbs, where you push tells you what kind of verb it is. If you push the small word at the start, UM, AUS, AN, EIN, it is separable, and ge goes in the middle. If you push the stem, beKOMmen, verKAUfen, there is no ge at all. Your ear can help you spell.
cards.lead: You now have two groups of prefix verbs. This card shows a simple way to tell them apart by ear: listen for the stress and clap it, so you know where ge goes.

deeper.text: The stress also helps you in the other direction. If you hear a separable verb, you know that in a normal sentence the prefix will go to the end of the sentence: Ich tausche die Hose um. If you hear an inseparable verb, it stays in one piece: Ich bekomme eine Tüte. So stress and grammar go together.

cards.title: Perfekt questions about shopping
cards.body: In a yes-no question haben comes first: Hast du die Jacke anprobiert? After a question word, haben is in part 2: Was hast du gekauft? The participle always stays at the very end. A dative pronoun goes between: Hat dir die Hose gefallen? Wer hat dir geholfen?

examples.why: W-word, haben in part 2, participle last.

Wer is the subject; dir stays before geholfen.

cards.more: You already know this bracket from chapter 10: the helper verb in one place, the participle at the very end. For questions you only move the helper. Yes-no question: haben goes to the front. W-question: haben goes right after the question word. The participle does not move. If there is a dative word, such as dir, it sits between the helper and the participle.
cards.lead: You can tell your shopping day. Now you ask about someone else's. This card shows the Perfekt questions you need, with the helper first and the participle last.

deeper.text: Verbs of movement use sein in the Perfekt, also in questions: Bist du ins Kaufhaus gegangen? Bist du mit dem Bus gefahren? The question works the same way: the helper goes first, the participle stays last. Only the helper is bist instead of hast. Listen for it, it tells you the verb moves.

cards.body: Berlin has huge Kaufhäuser and a famous shopping street, the Kurfürstendamm. On Sundays many people go to a Flohmarkt, for example in the Mauerpark. There you can find a Schnäppchen. Many Berliners bring their own Tüte. Learn these places and then read three Perfekt sentences about a shopping trip.

cards.more: A flea market is a little outdoor shop where people sell old clothes, books and many other things. In Berlin it is a real weekend plan: you walk around, look, talk and sometimes find a bargain. In the big Kaufhäuser the prices are fixed. At the Flohmarkt you can often ask for a better price. Bring a bag, because in Germany a Tüte is not always free.

deeper.text: A Schnäppchen is a bargain, a very good price. Germans love to say Das war ein Schnäppchen! It is a happy phrase. You can use war, which you know from chapter 10, for the past of sein. For the shopping itself you use the Perfekt: Ich habe ein Schnäppchen gefunden.

reading.title: Eine Jacke für die Party
reading.text:
Mira und Ben sind in Berlin. Anna und Leon sind auch da. Am Samstag hat Anna Geburtstag, und Mira braucht eine Jacke für die Party. Sie gehen ins Kaufhaus. Dort arbeitet ein Verkäufer. Er fragt: „Welche Jacke brauchen Sie?“ Mira sagt: „Diese Jacke ist rot, und diese Jacke ist grün. Welche Größe ist das?“ Der Verkäufer sagt: „Das ist Größe 38.“ Mira nimmt diese Jacke hier. Sie ist grün und günstig.
Ben trägt immer einen Pullover und eine Hose. Sie sind schwarz. Er sagt: „Ich brauche keinen Mantel, aber ich nehme diesen Schal.“ Der Schal ist auch schwarz. Mira lacht: „Ben, welche Farbe ist das? Schwarz!“

reading.title: Frau Weber im Kaufhaus
reading.text:
Frau Weber ist heute im Kaufhaus. Sie braucht einen Mantel und möchte einen Rock umtauschen. Eine Verkäuferin arbeitet in der Damenabteilung. Sie fragt: „Kann ich Ihnen helfen?“ Frau Weber sucht einen Mantel in Größe 40. Die Verkäuferin zeigt ihr einen Mantel in Blau. Sie probiert ihn in der Umkleidekabine an. Er passt ihr gut und ist im Angebot. Dann fragt sie: „Wo finde ich die Schuhabteilung?“ Die Verkäuferin sagt: „Im zweiten Stock.“

Am Abend schreibt sie an Leon: „Ich habe einen Mantel gekauft und den Rock umgetauscht. Die Verkäuferin hat mir geholfen. Der Mantel hat mir gut gefallen. Die Schuhe habe ich nicht gekauft.“
